Senses.Explanation: Literally “to bite and chew” (咬嚼), the term is attested 209 times in 109 allowlisted texts. Chan records extend the bodily action to sayings and public cases: one teacher tells beginners to “chew over a ready-made sentence that cannot be knocked down” and repeats “chew it over, chew it over” (咬嚼來、咬嚼去); the same record says Wujin spent his whole life unable to chew through “the bowl-carrying public case” (托缽公案). Other comments use the resistance of food as an explicit comparison: a saying can be “unable to be chewed through” (咬嚼不破), while Donglin offers only “wooden-slat soup and iron-nail rice—chew as you will” (木札羹、鉄釘飯，任汝咬嚼). The record also issues the opposite verdict, “strictly avoid chewing” (切忌咬嚼), after the answer “a thousand-year peach pit.”
Senses.Note: The Zen deviation is ordinary mastication used as a verb for sustained handling of a sentence, saying, or public case, with edible and inedible images kept visible. The corpus's affirmative instruction and prohibition are different appraisals of the same act, not separate senses. No independent high-value literal meal occurrence was found that would justify splitting actual eating from this lexicalized use.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “cut the cat.” This graph form occurs 156 times in 53 allowlisted texts and is an orthographic variant of “cut the cat” (斬貓), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts it in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase is used as a case title, a monk's question, a subject for verse, and a later master's cited precedent. One later exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; the master tells that questioner to repent. The exchange attests that the corpus itself places the case beside the rule against killing, but it does not state why Nanquan acted. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports that students call Guizong's snake-cutting and Nanquan's cat-cutting “timely wondrous function” or “great function appears, not retaining rules,” and explicitly says neither label gives the account.
Senses.Note: The simplified-looking graph for “cat” (猫) is a historical orthographic form alongside the other “cat” graph (貓) in the corpus. The two forms are separate searchable articles but carry the same case sense. The entry reports the explicit precept question and Dahui's rejection; it does not supply an unrecorded rationale for the killing.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, cut (斬) kudzu-and-wisteria creepers (葛藤). The parent image names verbal entanglement in Chan records, but this exact compound is very thin and occurs only in late framing prose. One text praises a master for effacing forms and cutting vine-tangle; a preface says that Linji's staff and shout cut all vine-tangle; a biographical preface pairs cutting vine-tangle with destroying thorn thickets. The Zen deviation comes from the established Chan use of creepers for entangling words, here made the object of cutting. Unlike the much commoner longer forms 'cut off the vine-tangle' and 'sever the vine-tangle,' the exact phrase is not attested in this concordance as a live-exchange command, so this entry does not present it as one.
Senses.Note: Exact-form count: 3 hits in 3 allowlisted texts, all curated. One late paratextual sense, mechanically multi-source but narrowly stated. Family checked against vine-tangle (葛藤), cut off the vine-tangle (斬斷葛藤: 16 hits in 15 texts), and sever the vine-tangle (截斷葛藤: 100 hits in 70 texts). Evidence from those longer forms is not assigned to this exact headword.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'cut the snake.' In the Chan corpus the expression is chiefly a compact reference to Guizong Zhichang's public case: he cut a passing snake with a hoe, a lecture monk called him coarse, Guizong raised the hoe as 'coarse,' made a cutting gesture as 'fine,' and asked where the monk had seen him cut the snake. Later masters ask about 'the old man's snake-cutting,' pair it with Nanquan cutting the cat and Dasui burning the clearing, turn 'the snake-cutter' into a stock agent noun, and compare Guizong's act with raising the whisk. The case is also explicitly challenged from the precepts: records ask why Guizong cut the snake when killing living beings is a major precept or when a precept-keeper will not tread on living grass. One answer tells the questioner to repent; another asks, 'is it cutting, or is it killing?' A sermon quoting the rule to rescue animals from killing then asks what could have saved Guizong's snake. The corpus does not call this snake poisonous and does not say it threatened the community.
Senses.Note: The exact expression occurs 137 times in 65 allowlisted texts, across core case retellings, public questions, sermons, verse, and commentarial collections. Its plain verbal sense and case-label use name the same act, so item 8 does not require a split. The later record supplies incompatible appraisals rather than different referents: one verse calls the cutting compassion, Dahui rejects familiar functional explanations, and Tianran condemns imitating the case as license for unrestrained conduct. They remain reported evidence within one sense, not a menu of dictionary readings.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “cut the cat.” This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 allowlisted texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; the master tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”
Senses.Note: The two cat graphs (貓/猫) are orthographic variants and receive separate searchable articles with one shared case sense. The entry preserves the explicit precept challenges and refusals without deciding why Nanquan acted.
